overview: The atlas gives “Nunavik” a 1492-1500 polygon and calls it a state, but the name and legal geography must not be projected backward as a fifteenth-century government. Nunavik Inuit organizations describe a living homeland in northern Québec. The decoded atlas shape is much rougher: it excludes several present Nunavik communities, includes Schefferville below the modern region, overlaps a broad Inuit layer, and touches an Eeyou Istchee layer. This card therefore follows Inuit history in the region around 1492 while treating the colored line as an approximate reconstruction, not a surveyed frontier. The Parnasimautik consultation report presents archaeological evidence for long Inuit use and describes seasonal travel, camps, caribou, seals, fish, birds, and berries before sustained European contact. Its page describes more established winter camps of extended families in igloos and summer family groups spreading along coasts and river valleys. More specific site evidence appears below. Dated sources examine shelters, boats, family work, stories, language, care, and sanitation rather than silently backfilling later memories. The 1500 endpoint is a software seam. Nunavimmiut families, language, culture, and institutions continue.

periods.title: An atlas layer appears
periods.summary: The 1492 snapshot introduces one 130-position polygon for this exact id. It has no capital, ruler, assembly, founding act, or surveyed boundary. This and the next seven one-year slices are editorial reading aids; the atlas provides an interval, not eight annual chronicles or evidence that Nunavik was a state.

periods.title: A winter house brackets the interval
periods.summary: No source identifies a special event in 1493. At Paaliup Qarmangit 1, however, calibrated dates place Thule-Inuit use of a single-family semi-subterranean winter dwelling in 1466-1642, a range that securely includes the atlas interval. Archaeology supports household presence, while its broad probability range cannot date an individual meal or occupant.

periods.title: Seasonal movement organized work
periods.summary: The atlas records no 1494 migration. Taamusi Qumaq’s 1992 account instead remembers rivers as drinking places, fisheries, and routes, with winter snow houses, summer skin tents, and dogs helping travel. It is valuable named testimony about earlier lifeways, yet not an eyewitness diary for one fifteenth-century year.

periods.title: Households engineered mobility
periods.summary: Nothing marks 1495 as the invention of a qajaq. Avataq’s tool guide instead sets boats beside harpoons, fish spears, lamps, knives, and skin-working equipment. The evidence reveals a connected technical system adapted to water, ice, prey, fuel, and household work, without assigning every listed form to precisely this year.

periods.title: Place names carried knowledge
periods.summary: No dated 1496 naming event is known. Nunavik elders directed Avataq to collect names, confirm their local use, and seek their appearance on official maps. That modern project demonstrates how names carry enduring geographic knowledge; it does not prove when each name arose or draw an exclusive fifteenth-century border.

periods.title: Birth care depended on people
periods.summary: The atlas supplies no 1497 birth record. Avataq’s later interview archive describes experienced midwives assisting labor and families providing newborn and maternal care. It documents women’s expertise and support, but the evidence was gathered centuries afterward and includes treatments unsafe today; it cannot reconstruct one delivery in this editorial year.

periods.title: Speech, story, and memory mattered
periods.summary: No 1498 manuscript survives from this layer. Avataq’s language history describes stories, songs, myths, and accounts carried orally during long winter nights, teaching children, values, hunts, seasons, and entertainment. Audiences corrected narrators who departed from remembered forms. That is evidence for disciplined transmission, not word-for-word access to a 1498 performance.

periods.title: The color changes; people continue
periods.summary: In 1500 the exact polygon disappears, and several sampled points are repainted as “Thule”; by 1530 many receive an unrelated broad “Naskapi-Innu” layer. The files record no conquest, evacuation, or collective death. Avataq’s living language work makes the safer conclusion plain: map categories change while Nunavimmiut continuity persists.

sections.title: Read the atlas boundary with care

items.text: The imported index names Nunavik, dates it approximately 1492-1500, and coverage calls it a state with one border file. Its summary describes today’s region. Those database fields document an unfinished atlas entry; they do not establish a fifteenth-century capital, legislature, treaty line, or centralized Nunavik polity.

Makivvik describes modern Nunavik above the 55th parallel, 14 coastal villages, and a separate marine land-claims region containing shared-use areas with Nunavut Inuit and Cree. Those precise modern arrangements are crucial today, but they cannot serve as the legal key for interpreting an approximate polygon labeled 1492.

Decoded from the 1492 topology, the feature is one Polygon with one ring and 130 stored positions. Its bounding box runs about 78.93° to 63.24° west and 54.32° to 62.52° north. It shares two arcs with “inuit” and one with “eeyou-istchee,” showing layered atlas categories.

Point tests expose the reconstruction’s limits. Kuujjuaq and Inukjuak fall inside, but Kangiqsualujjuaq, Quaqtaq, Ivujivik, Akulivik, and Umiujaq do not; Schefferville does. Makivvik lists all those coastal places except Schefferville within modern Nunavik. The polygon is therefore neither a reliable community inventory nor a modern boundary.

The exact id occurs only in 1492 among 50 audited snapshots. At 1500 it vanishes while a broad “thule” layer covers many probes; 1530 repaints several again. These pixels cannot identify migration, conquest, ethnic replacement, or consent. They reveal the atlas editor’s changing categories, not an ending experienced by families.

sections.title: Let archaeology show presence without inventing names

items.text: Paaliup Qarmangit 1 preserves a single-family, semi-subterranean Thule-Inuit winter house. Researchers date two use ranges to 1317-1413 and 1466-1642 calibrated CE; the second brackets 1492. Building material, food, and water helped make the location useful, while wind, snow, and later disturbance reshaped its deposits.

At JfEl-10 near Quaqtaq, revised dates place Thule Inuit occupation after Dorset occupation rather than proving both groups lived there together. Faunal and environmental evidence points to fall or winter marine-mammal hunting. A site’s mixed remains can therefore reflect different visits and post-depositional processes, not one blended household.

Nunaingok contains semi-subterranean dwellings and nearly four millennia of material, from Pre-Dorset deposits to the 1930s. Excavators recorded an entry hall and sleeping platform and collected thousands of artifacts. Because generations reused the peninsula, the whole assemblage cannot be flattened into a single “1492 Inuit house.”

From 1985 to 1987, Avataq surveyed five-kilometre zones around nine proposed airport projects, finding more than 250 sites from multiple periods, excavating four, and safeguarding threatened remains. Modern construction unexpectedly prompted a major discovery program: an airport survey became a time machine, although archaeologists still had to separate its many dates.

A 1983 Nunavik elders’ resolution led to Avataq’s Archaeology Department in 1985. Its mandate covers Inuit, ancestors, and predecessors, and its field program trains young Inuit alongside archaeologists. This community authority matters: archaeological expertise is not simply outsiders naming old objects, and archaeological labels are not modern ethnic borders.

sections.title: Follow seasons, food, water, and local ecology

items.text: Nunavik Parks describes small autonomous family groups moving seasonally for food at early European contact. Hunting, fishing, and gathering included caribou, fish, marine mammals, eggs, and berries. That regional outline fits a mobile economy, but it cannot identify the exact menu, party size, or route of one household in 1492.

Taamusi Qumaq wrote in 1992 that rivers supplied drinking water, fish, and travel routes. Winter snow and summer sun connected shelter and water, while skin tents served warmer seasons. His dated voice preserves lived knowledge; the card does not pretend he personally witnessed the fifteenth century.

Caribou and seals supplied more than meals: Nunavik Parks links them to shelter, clothing, and fuel as well as food. Fish, ptarmigan, eggs, and berries could broaden seasonal options. Availability varied, so “Arctic diet” should never become one repetitive plate served everywhere, every day, to every family.

Nunavik Parks places the igloo beside the qajaq, ulu, qulliq, fitted fur clothing, and detachable-headed harpoon as linked technologies for Arctic life. The list is useful because shelter was one part of a larger technical system. It still cannot supply the exact belongings or moving calendar of a 1492 household.

In a 1992 Kangirsuk portrait, Qumaq explained that Arctic char flesh differed between Ungava and Hudson coasts because the fish ate different prey. He also described fishing through winter ice with a kakivak. It is a delightful ecological lesson: even neighboring char did not all read the same menu.

sections.title: Engineer shelter, clothing, boats, and tools

items.text: Avataq defines the amautik as a woman’s coat with a back pouch for carrying a baby, and annuraat as skin clothing made from caribou, seal, dog, or eiderdown. Clothing joined thermal engineering with caregiving. The definitions document forms and materials, not who sewed every garment or wore one in 1492.

A kakivak used a central point and curved, barbed ivory side pieces to keep a speared fish from slipping away. The unaaq served seal hunting in summer and winter; the half-moon ulu was associated with women’s work. Each compact tool embodied knowledge of material, prey, season, and motion.

Puurtaq participants remembered about a thousand named pieces in a qajaq frame, each shaped from carefully chosen, scarce driftwood. The number should be read as community memory, not a parts catalogue for every ancient boat. Still, it captures the precision required before one sealskin ever touched the frame.

Sealskins for qajaqs were dehaired, softened, and joined with specialized stitches that could not leak. The memory project assigns hunting, frame building, sewing, helping, and cooking across a gathered work group. A finished boat was therefore a social achievement as well as a sleek piece of transport technology.

The qulliq burned marine-mammal fat for heat, light, drying clothes, and hot drinks. Qamutiik carried heavy loads behind dogs, while an umiaq moved people, tents, dogs, and equipment and was usually operated by women. These technologies turned local animal, stone, skin, and travel knowledge into household infrastructure.

sections.title: Meet families, workmates, singers, and namesakes

items.text: Puurtaq memories describe children helping mothers and grandparents, clearing snow, and assisting with animal skins while adults hunted, sewed, and collected driftwood. This is later oral history, not a census of 1492 chores. It nevertheless corrects the cartoon of children merely watching grown-ups perform Arctic survival.

Puurtaq memories describe adults and children pitching in when qajaqs were built, after women gathered scarce shoreline driftwood. The same page remembers children helping mothers and grandparents and women sewing by qulliq light. Work was social and intergenerational, although this later testimony cannot assign one crew list to 1492.

Avataq’s genealogy project records customary adoption without written paperwork and preserves both biological and adoptive family connections. It also notes specific Inuktitut sibling terms. These later research methods show why a family cannot be reconstructed from one surname or household list, much less projected unchanged across five centuries.

The genealogy guide describes sauniq, namesake relationships formed when children received an ancestor’s or elder’s name. Names could carry social connections alongside biological and adoptive kinship. The project documents a northern custom, while acknowledging change; it does not give us the names or family tree of an unidentified 1492 household.

Nunavik katajjaniq is a friendly, competitive throat-singing game commonly performed by two women. Sounds overlap and can echo wind, water, animals, and daily life; a round ends when someone gasps or laughs. Its transmission links play, environmental listening, women’s knowledge, festivals, and soothing children.

sections.title: Learn through stories, elders, places, and practice

items.text: Avataq’s language history says long winter nights carried stories, myths, songs, hunts, seasonal events, moral teaching, and entertainment. Narrators memorized established structures, and listeners corrected departures. Oral learning was therefore active scholarship with an alert audience, not a fuzzy game of telephone in which every version drifted unnoticed.

Because the 1492 layer has no securely dated local manuscript, speech and material evidence must carry the history. Avataq dates Latin-alphabet missionary writing to the 1700s in Greenland and Labrador and Peck’s Inuktitut syllabic adaptation to the late 1800s. Those milestones cannot be moved backward to decorate this interval.

Nunavik elders asked Avataq to collect Inuit place names and confirm their use with local communities, then pursue maps and a gazetteer. Their resolution emphasized permanence and cultural value. Locally confirmed names make a map more meaningful than an imported blank polygon, but they do not automatically become exclusive boundary markers.

Avataq’s excavation school at Nunaingok gave Inuit students advanced field training, while its wider youth program pairs students with archaeologists. That is education about the past through careful digging, recording, and interpretation. It also gives Nunavimmiut tools to question outsiders’ labels instead of receiving archaeology as a finished story.

A Kativik School Board resource describes modern schooling in which children begin subjects in Inuktitut and Inuit educators help create and test classroom materials. This is twentieth- and twenty-first-century institutional education, not a fifteenth-century classroom. It demonstrates continuity through adaptation rather than a timeless, unchanged teaching system.

sections.title: Hear Inuktitut and read one carefully dated sample

items.text: Avataq notes phonetic and lexical differences between Nunavik’s Hudson Bay and Ungava coasts, alongside wider Arctic variation. One printed sample cannot represent every community voice. Spoken Inuktitut long predates the writing system; spelling is a useful technology for language, not the starting date of the language itself.

Written sample: “ᓇᑦᓯᖅ”; alphabetic transliteration “natsiq”; meaning “ringed seal.” Nunavik-IcE prints the syllables spaced as “ᓇ ᑦ ᓯ ᖅ,” while Avataq supplies the meaning. This is a secure modern teaching example, not an inscription or manuscript from the atlas’s dated 1492 map interval.

Nunavik’s standard orthography has alphabetic qaliujaarpait and syllabic qaniujaarpait versions with systematic correspondences. In “natsiq,” the small final signs write consonants inside a cluster and at the word’s end. The example shows how sound analysis and visual design work together rather than merely swapping decorative symbols.

Kativik’s lesson dates syllabics to nineteenth-century missionary work, credits Edmund Peck with spreading the system from the 1870s, and says Inuit and linguists refined it in the 1970s. Today’s standard closely follows the 1976 Inuit Tapirisat standard. Every date is centuries after this card’s atlas interval.

Nunavik elders established Avataq’s language commission in 1984. The department supports terminology workshops, dictionaries, and teaching, including Taamusi Qumaq’s major dictionary. These are modern achievements by living language stewards. They show why a card should preserve exact Inuktitut forms and resist treating language as an archaeological relic.

sections.title: Describe medicine and caregiving without prescribing

items.text: Avataq’s medicine archive comes from 1983 group interviews with elders in all 14 northern Québec Inuit communities. Researchers found similarities, differences, and knowledge carried through kin links. That method makes the evidence rich but dated: it cannot certify that every recorded practice existed everywhere, or in exactly the same form, in 1492.

The archive says most people knew basic care while midwives and surgeons held more specialized knowledge. Expertise, talent, observation, and family practice could coexist without hospitals or textbooks. This describes a social pattern from later testimony; it is not permission to recreate a procedure or assume every household had an identical healer.

One elder humorously remembered rubbing cranberries into snow-blinded eyes as a child, causing frightening pain instead of relief. Avataq included the story as evidence of experimentation and contradiction. Its kid-friendly lesson is excellent: “traditional” does not mean “try this yourself,” and a painful mistake can still teach caution.

Avataq’s birth archive says trained or experienced midwives assisted labor and recorded later memories of newborn and maternal care. The account matters for women’s expertise and family support, but several described treatments would be unsafe today. This card records that care existed; it offers no diagnosis, dose, or home-birth instruction.

An amautik carried a baby in a warm back pouch while leaving an adult mobile. That design joins thermal protection, transport, closeness, and caregiving in one garment. The lexicon securely defines the form, but it cannot tell us which infant, caregiver, stitching pattern, or daily routine belonged to an unidentified 1492 household.

sections.title: Handle water, cleaning, waste, and toilets honestly

items.text: Qumaq called rivers precious because people drank from them, caught fish there, and traveled them. He also remembered snow as shelter and a source of clear water. This 1992 account conveys relationship and practical value, while a modern health study warns that source and storage conditions now require monitoring.

Puurtaq participants remembered family-sized igloos cleaned daily: sleeping platforms were smoothed, ice windows scraped, and dirty, sooty, or urine-marked snow removed and replaced. The worst chore was cleaning floor cracks. A snow house was not magically self-cleaning; keeping it bright required regular, unglamorous maintenance.

Children fetched water and carried out the waste bucket even in severe cold, then repeated those chores for grandparents and elderly neighbors. This later memory joins sanitation with intergenerational care. It should not be assigned automatically to every 1492 household, but it supplies unusually direct evidence about who did necessary work.

Neither the Paaliup house study nor Avataq’s long Nunaingok summary identifies a fifteenth-century latrine, sewer, privy, or fixed toilet rule. Refuse deposits and occupied floors need contextual analysis before receiving a bathroom label. The honest answer for a 1492 toilet is therefore: evidence remains insufficient at these cited sites.

Current Nunavik Parks guidance tells backcountry visitors to dig cat holes 15-20 centimetres deep at least 70 metres from water, camp, and trails, then pack out paper. That is modern conservation guidance, not ancient custom. The funny part is timelessly relatable: even an epic landscape still needs a bathroom plan.

Qajaq, umiaq, kakivak, unaaq, ulu, qulliq, qamutiik, fitted skin clothing, and seasonal shelters form a system rather than a gadget list. Avataq’s tool descriptions show knowledge of buoyancy, waterproof stitching, leverage, fuel, insulation, prey behavior, and transport. Survival depended on engineering, skilled maintenance, and coordination.

The Puurtaq qajaq account joins scarce driftwood, precise angles, specialized waterproof stitches, sealskin preparation, stored provisions, celebration, portage, dogs, and family travel. Its achievement is the whole production network. “About a thousand named pieces” also gives children a satisfying answer: yes, boat-building homework could be enormous.

Avataq’s place-name program turns elders’ knowledge into locally checked maps and gazetteers, seeking official recognition and daily use. This is both cultural preservation and geographic infrastructure. A map becomes more useful when it carries generations of named experience, although publication cannot replace the speakers and communities who interpret those names.

A 2003-2004 study found frequently used brook, lake, and river collection sites generally good in most villages, while household storage containers showed more contamination. Researchers recommended monitoring, warnings, better wastewater systems, and nursing involvement. Modern science here did not dismiss local water use; it identified where present-day risks concentrated.

Avataq now cares for archaeology, archives, art, and ethnography. Its archive holds hundreds of oral histories, historic photographs, drawings, medicine interviews, and Puurtaq recordings; its collections preserve both practical ingenuity and artistic interpretation. Stewardship is an achievement in its own right because evidence survives through community choices, cataloguing, teaching, and access.

ending.text: The atlas stops drawing this exact id in 1500. It supplies no battle, treaty, epidemic, forced migration, political collapse, or named successor. Its next snapshot paints many sampled places “Thule,” and the following one repaints several again; those categories are inconsistent enough to be evidence about the map, not a collective ending. Nunavimmiut did not vanish at the seam. Later centuries brought sustained European trade, missions, imposed settlement, schooling, government administration, land claims, and new institutions, each requiring its own dates and sources. Today Avataq Cultural Institute’s Nunavik Inuit mandate supports language, elders, youth, archaeology, archives, art, place names, and cultural knowledge. The modern legal region and marine agreements also remain distinct from the rough historical-basemap polygon. This card therefore closes with living continuity. Its evidence reaches 1492 most securely through calibrated archaeology and reaches remembered lifeways through carefully dated community testimony. The software layer ended; families, spoken Inuktitut, written Inuktitut, knowledge, humor, creativity, and responsibilities to land, water, animals, ancestors, and future generations continue.
